mcqs.question: 1,000 requests are measured: 990 take 50ms and 10 take 5,000ms. The mean latency is roughly 99.5ms. What does this mean hide?
options: That 1% of users experienced latency roughly 100x worse than the rest, which the mean doesn't reveal at all
Nothing significant — the mean is a reliable summary of any latency distribution
That the median must also be close to 5,000ms
That the measurement itself is invalid due to insufficient sample size
mcqs.explanation: The mean is dominated by the bulk of fast requests and gives no visibility into the tail — 1% of users had a dramatically worse experience that a mean of ~99.5ms completely obscures. This is exactly why percentiles, not the mean, are the standard way to report latency.

mcqs.question: A request depends on 10 independent downstream calls, each with a 1% chance of hitting its own p99-or-worse latency. Roughly what is the chance the overall request is dragged into its tail by at least one of them?
options: About 1%, the same as any single call, since percentiles compose linearly
About 10%, since it's simply 10 times 1%
About 0.01%, since all ten would need to be unlucky simultaneously
Roughly 9.6% — the chance at least one of ten independent 1%-probability events occurs is 1 minus (0.99)^10
mcqs.explanation: The overall response waits on the slowest of the ten independent calls, so the chance of being dragged into the tail is 1 − (0.99)^10 ≈ 9.6% — almost 10x higher than any individual call's own 1% tail probability. This is the 'tail at scale' effect that fan-out creates.

mcqs.question: A request makes five downstream calls: two that the response must wait on (auth check, database read) and three optional enrichment calls whose results aren't needed until later. Which calls are on the critical path?
options: Only the auth check and database read — the two the response must wait on, regardless of how slow the other three are
All five, since the request makes five total downstream calls
None of them, since critical path only applies to single-threaded code
Only the slowest of the five, whichever one that happens to be on a given request
mcqs.explanation: The critical path is the sequence of operations that must complete before the response can be sent — the three optional enrichment calls aren't on it no matter how slow they are, since they don't block the response. Optimizing them wouldn't help latency at all; only the auth check and database read matter for that.

mcqs.question: A system's CPU utilization rises from 75% to 92%. Using the M/M/1 queueing approximation (wait scales with ρ/(1−ρ)), roughly how does the queueing-driven latency change?
options: It increases modestly, roughly proportional to the 17-point utilization increase
It stays about the same, since both values are well under 100%
It decreases, since higher utilization means the system is using its resources more efficiently
It increases sharply and disproportionately — the ρ/(1−ρ) factor goes from 3 at 75% to 11.5 at 92%, nearly 4x worse from a 17-point utilization change
mcqs.explanation: The queueing factor is non-linear: at ρ=0.75 it's 0.75/0.25=3, at ρ=0.92 it's 0.92/0.08=11.5 — nearly a 4x jump from a utilization increase that looks modest on a dashboard. This is why running near saturation causes latency to explode well before utilization hits 100%.

mcqs.question: A service is experiencing a latency spike under load. What's the practical difference between fixing it by adding capacity versus reducing work per request?
options: Adding capacity is a fast, often minutes-scale response (e.g., autoscaling) that lowers utilization directly, while reducing work per request is a slower engineering fix but removes the underlying cost going forward — the two are complementary, not competing
The two approaches are functionally identical and interchangeable in every case
Reducing work per request is always faster to deploy than adding capacity
Adding capacity permanently fixes the root cause, making work-reduction unnecessary
mcqs.explanation: Capacity is the fast lever — often deployable in minutes via autoscaling — while reducing work per request takes real engineering time but removes the underlying demand for capacity permanently. Mature systems use both: capacity as the immediate response, work-reduction as the durable fix.

mcqs.question: A team adds a cache lookup on every request to speed up the common case. Average latency improves, but p99 gets worse. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The monitoring dashboard is misconfigured and the p99 figure is inaccurate

Cache hits (the large majority) got faster, while cache misses — which were probably already slower — now also pay the cache lookup's overhead on top of the original cost, worsening the tail even as the mean improves
Caches always improve average latency at the direct expense of correctness
p99 latency is unrelated to any single optimization and can be ignored as noise
mcqs.explanation: An optimization that helps the common case at a small fixed cost to every request can make the average look better while making the tail worse, because the tail is dominated by exactly the requests (cache misses) that don't get the benefit but still pay the added cost. Checking percentiles, not just the mean, catches this before it ships.
